interest: This file offers a unique glimpse into grassroots American commercial interest in post-war occupied Japan, illustrating how private citizens sought to revive or initiate specialized trans-Pacific agricultural arrangements during the Allied occupation. It is particularly interesting for its reference to the 'Croft Lily' (a prominent commercial Easter lily cultivar) and for showing the administrative pathways created by the State Department and SCAP, which directed private trade inquiries to Japan's newly established Board of Trade (Bōeki-chō) while coordinating with the U.S. Department of Agriculture on plant quarantine and re-import controls.
keywords: Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs
overview: This file consists of correspondence from May and June 1948 between H. W. 'Lee' Croft, the Sheriff of Pierce County, Washington, and the U.S. Department of State concerning commercial horticultural arrangements with occupied Japan. Croft inquired about procedures for contracting with Japanese growers or the Japanese government to ship Lily of the Valley and Croft lily bulbs to Japan for propagation and subsequent return to the United States. In reply, Roswell H. Whitman, Acting Chief of the Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs, advised Croft to contact the Japanese Board of Trade (Bōeki-chō) in Tokyo to locate a suitable commercial dealer and recommended consulting the U.S. Department of Agriculture regarding plant re-import regulations.

subfiles.summary: H. W. Croft, Sheriff of Pierce County, Washington, writes to the Bureau of Foreign Affairs in Washington, D.C., seeking guidance on how to establish a contract with Japanese entities or the Japanese Government. He explains that he wishes to ship Lily of the Valley and Croft Lily bulbs to Japan for cultivation and have the multiplied yield returned to him. Noting reports that such arrangements are already taking place, he asks for contact information and particulars.

subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman of the Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs responds to H. W. Croft's May 31 inquiry regarding bulb trade with Japan. He suggests that Croft write to the Japanese Board of Trade (Bōeki-chō) in Tokyo to be connected with a dealer familiar with custom propagation contracts. Whitman also cautions Croft to verify re-import regulations with the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
